newsitem.title: BERMUDA: CRICKET - Astle to bite the patience bullet.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET - Astle to bite the patience bullet.

text.p: HAMILTON, March 17 - Canterbury batsman Nathan Astle completed his test programme for the season with a half-century but he knows a lot of work needs to be done before he cements a place in the New Zealand middle order, NZPA reports.
Astle's 52 on the third day of the second test against Sri Lanka on Sunday was not an innings he will look back on fondly, but at least it helped New Zealand set Sri Lanka a stiff victory target.
New Zealand made 273 in their second innings, leaving Sri Lanka requiring an unlikely 326 runs to win the game and square the two-match rubber.
Sri Lanka made a poor start on a wearing pitch and resume this morning on 20 for two facing a searching examination of their patience to save the match.
Patience is a quality Astle admits he could do with more of when he's at the crease. Impetuosity has cost him dearly this season, his second full term on the international stage.
His knock yesterday was riddled with a series of ambitious but unrealistic wafts at the ball outside offstump. He mostly hit thin air as he played and missed more often than he cares to remember.
It has been a tendency of Astle's to chase the ball outside offstump all season, and it has translated into a significant downgrading of his batting.

Seven tests this summer have netted him just 266 runs at an average of 22. That marks a big slump on his returns in 1995-96 when he seemingly made the No 5 position his own by hitting 367 runs, including two glorious centuries in the West Indies, in four tests at a world-class average of nearly 46.

Astle, 25, remains New Zealand's first-choice opening batsman for one-day matches, but he has been dismissed for 11 or less eight times in 13 innings in tests this season, and he admits he has to learn to curb his natural aggression for the test arena.
"I have to work a lot harder at being patient," he said.
"(Coach) Steve Rixon has had a talk to me about that and I've known that for a while now.
"I have to work harder on perfecting the patience part of my cricket.
"It is a matter of me curbing my natural game and being more selective in the shots I play.
"I was playing at balls two or three feet outside offstump today and, with the angle the left arm bowlers were bowling at, that's just ridiculous to try to hit those."

Astle, whose seasonal statistics were inflated by his magnificent, unbeaten 103 to save the first test against England in Auckland in late January, always knew his second season at international level was going to test him.
"It's been a tough second year and I was expecting it to be. I had a pretty good season last year and it is hard to backup those sorts of seasons," he said.
"I probably haven't worked as hard as I should have and I'll have to look at that when this season finishes and I reassess things for next year."

Astle's was the third half-century in New Zealand's 273 following earlier, much better controlled contributions of opener Bryan Young, who made 62 and captain Stephen Fleming, who was his usual elegant, languid self when making 59.

A fiesty last-wicket stand of 30 between Simon Doull, who made 25 from just 29 deliveries, and Heath Davis carried New Zealand's lead past the 300-mark, which was an important psychological barrier at Trust Bank Park.
No team have topped 300 here all summer, and it is hardly surprising that groundsman Ian McKendry has received permission to dig up the entire block this winter.
The pitch here is on a base of Naike clay from near Huntly which normally needs to be relaid every three years. It has been seven years since the Trust Bank Park pitch has been dug up and relaid.
For Sri Lankan coach Bruce Yardley, who said the pitch was not up to the standards required for a test match, the renovations cannot happen in time to save his side from likely defeat.

The state of the pitch dominated talk before this game following a series of extraordinary results in Hamilton this season, including Northern Districts seam bowler Alex Tait's record first-class match haul of 16 for 130 against Auckland in a match when his own team folded for a mere 32 in their second innings.
"It was wet on the first day. We would have batted first on it because we had absolutely no idea what it was going to do and it's often better to bat first in situations like that," Yardley said.
